The road as a window manager — Tier 1

Status: `spec`; standalone Linux Tier 1 and two-app handoff proofs implemented. An initial road surface is integrated into Super in a separate window; the full road-shell product is not implemented. Six decisions remain open in §13. The scope ruling in §1 is Travis's, 2026-09-10. Everything downstream of it is a proposal.

Author: Claude, 2026-09-10. Companion to PAPER_ROADS.md (the pane), OP_VOCABULARY_DRAFT.md (the seam), and super/docs/app/DESKTOP_SHELL.md (the host).

Revised 2026-09-10 after review. Five things were tightened and each is recorded as a correction in DOCTRINE rather than edited away: the live budget is separate from pose eligibility (§4.1); a sign says three things, not one (§5.1); the capability layer is only half the authority boundary (§6.1); the liveness wording was too absolute (§10.1); and "macOS is easier" is a hypothesis with a test list (§11). §12 is now the single narrow proof to build before anything accumulates around it.

0. The one-line version

A road that manages web apps needs no new operating system, and no new primitive. The Tauri host, the multi-webview primitive, the per-pane authority boundary, the slot allocator, the op seam, and the three-tier residency ladder all exist and are measured. What does not exist is a fourth tier — `live` — and the manifest that says which app may stand where.

1. What was asked, and what was ruled

Asked: could a Tauri app host other apps on a T&R road, with entrance signs, exit ramps and advert billboards, acting as a load balancer for CD-compatible apps — and would it run on a Mac.

Ruled: Tier 1 only. An app on the road is a webview. Not a streamed native window (compositor-proxy's job, and it stays compositor-proxy's job), and not somebody else's Mac window driven through the Accessibility API. This ruling is what makes the macOS answer cheap and the authority answer tractable, and §11 and §6 are downstream of it.

The consequence to state plainly: an application that is not a web application cannot stand on this road. foot, xterm, Firefox-as-a-guest-window are Tier 2 and reach the road only the way they do today, through compositor-proxy into a billboard texture. Tier 1 does not replace that path and does not compete with it.

2. What already exists — measured, so no session re-derives it

Five things. Each is in the tree today; each is cited so this document can be checked rather than believed.

2.1 The Tauri host, with the unstable primitive already on and already justified

super/cockpit/ is a Tauri v2 desktop application. super/cockpit/Cargo.toml:17 reads tauri = { version = "2", features = ["unstable"] }, and the six comment lines above it say why in the product's own words:

unstable is what gates Window::add_child and WebviewBuilder — the multi-webview-per-window primitive. Super's browser, Motor and game panes are that primitive … It is the only reason the feature is on.

super/cockpit/src/main.rs:80 draws the topology it expects — WebView "main" the cockpit, WebView "browser" a page, WebView "machine" a Motor surface. This document is that diagram with a road under it.

2.2 An external URL, in a child webview, at an arbitrary rect, with a policy on it

super/cockpit/src/preview.rs:138 already calls add_child with WebviewUrl::External(url), on_navigation(allowed) and on_new_window(|_, _| NewWindowResponse::Deny), positions it from a caller-supplied rect, validates that rect against the window's own size, and can hide/close/re-navigate it.

That is an app pane. It exists. The remaining work is not the mechanism — it is where the rect comes from and who is allowed to ask for it.

2.3 The per-pane authority boundary, held by a gate

super/cockpit/capabilities/default.json grants webviews: ["main"] with no `windows` key at all, and its description records why:

tauri's resolver is an OR over the two lists (ipc/authority.rs, resolve_access), so a pane hosted INSIDE the cockpit window would have inherited all of this.

capabilities/terminal.json is the shape a pane takes: three permissions, webviews: ["terminal"], no intent, no core permission, no fourth command. tools/check-webview-acl.mjs fails if windows returns, and reconciles three lists that can each drift alone — generate_handler! (registered), build.rs AppManifest::commands (in the ACL), and capabilities/ (granted). A command registered but absent from build.rs fails open.

Upstream now says the same thing: "On multiwebview windows, prefer specifying webviews and omitting windows for a fine grained access control."

2.4 The slot allocator — already the placement half of a load balancer

RRABBIT/m2/world.js holds it and it is not a sketch:

DASH_PITCH = 180 (l.92)the addressable grid
SLOT_GAP = 4, SLOT_FIRST (l.220, l.227)window↔window spacing; the first legal dash
slotAt(district, side, dash) (l.237)what stands here — already four occupant kinds
slotFree(…, kind, ignore) (l.258)may a window/ramp/paper/mail stand here
nextFreeSlot / nearestFreeSlot (l.294, l.302)forward-fill and outward-search

A fifth kind is an entry in these functions, not a new subsystem. The two spacing rules are deliberately not a shared footprint — PAPER_ROADS.md §22 falsified the hypothesis that would have widened SLOT_GAP, so do not widen it here either.

2.5 The seam, built and survived its own falsification test

RRABBIT/m2/ops.js is apply(op) — one function every actor passes through. TABLE (l.41) is closed and currently holds 21 ops; register (l.127) injects the doing, which is what lets node test/ops.mjs exercise validation, refusal, logging and replay with no GL context.

PAPER_ROADS.md DOCTRINE records the result: "falsifiable, survived — the seam serves three consumers with no per-consumer branch, asserted mechanically rather than by inspection."

A road shell is a fourth consumer, and the strongest evidence yet for the pending ruling in `OP_VOCABULARY_DRAFT.md` §8. It is also the first consumer whose actor is another program.

3. The collision, and why the existing design already survives it

An OS child webview is an axis-aligned rectangle in window coordinates. It cannot be rotated 0.42 rad, cannot be perspective-projected, cannot receive a curve, and is composited by the OS above the page rather than into the WebGL scene. A three.js road cannot draw one.

This looks fatal for ten seconds, and then the spec answers it. docs/spec/README.md §1:

A window you are typing into is never at an angle.

and RRABBIT/m2/paper.js:279 already has the mechanism — the read tier's DOM object stands at the quad's own pose, in a CSS3D layer with its own scene and renderer but the same camera, "which is what makes reading a pane continuous with driving past it instead of a modal that replaces the world."

So the rule falls out rather than being imposed:

A live webview exists only in the read pose. At any other pose the app is a picture.

read / unread are already the ops for entering and leaving that pose (ops.js l.46–47), already plan-split correctly, and already carry resize, close and cast beside them (§17 of PAPER_ROADS.md, table 4 → 7). The live tier needs no new navigation verb.

4. The residency ladder — a fourth tier

paper.js opens with the tier discipline and the reason for it — "NOTHING EXPENSIVE IS ALLOCATED UNTIL A TIER ASKS FOR IT", after a first version cost ~1.07 MB of canvas per pane whether or not it would ever be read. Tier 1 adds one rung on top:

tiercostswhat it is
hiddennothingon another road; holds no pixels
carda cell in the shared atlas (1 texture / 96)a distant sign
paintown canvas, own texture, own materiala readable sign
`live`a WKWebView/WebKitGTK processthe app, running, in the read pose

`live` is the only tier with a process behind it. Each WKWebView gets its own WebContent process, and per-webview memory can run to 200+ MB for a heavy page. The ladder's whole job is to keep that number multiplied by a small integer.

4.1 Pose eligibility is not a resource budget

The first draft of this document said "`live` is bounded by pose, not by policy — one read pose, one live pane, by construction." That is wrong, and the shipped code already falsifies it. §17.1 of PAPER_ROADS.md records that an on-air pane must pin its paint tier — castKey is exempt from retiering, exactly as the read pane is — because watching a pane while driving away from it is the entire reason to cast one. So a tier already outlives its pose by design, and it was made to on purpose.

Two more reasons the pose cannot serve as the budget: promotion and demotion are asynchronous, so more than one pane can be eligible during a transition; and a hidden webview is not a paused webview (§10.4) — a demoted pane that has not been destroyed is still spending.

So the budget is a separate, explicit rule, and it needs three parts:

v1why
How many may be liveexactly 1the smallest number that can be reasoned about, and the only one that needs no eviction policy
When one is unloadedon leaving the read pose, unless pinned by castmatches the one exemption that already exists, rather than inventing a second
How its state survivesthe app's checkpoint/resume contract (§10.4)the shell cannot do this for the app, and must not claim to

N > 1 and a resident tier are both deliberately out of v1. Raising N is a resource ruling, not a rendering change, and it must be made against a measurement (§11) rather than against the fact that the panes happen to fit on screen.

Agent `rest`/`wake` stay separate from all of this — see §10.5. A pane's residency and an agent's quiescent/runnable are two livenesses and this document does not merge them.

5. The advert sign is published, not screenshotted

The card and paint tiers need a face, and the face cannot be a screenshot of the live pane. Two reasons, one measured and one structural:

  • Measured: neither wry nor core Tauri exposes a webview snapshot API — it is an open

feature request, served today only by community plugins.

  • Structural: a shell that samples its panes' pixels is a shell that can sample its panes'

pixels. The whole Wayland-side posture of this stack is that a surface's contents belong to its client.

So: an app's sign face is something the app declares, and the paint tier draws it with the same `{rect, line, text}` primitive set that survived a second format without widening (PAPER_ROADS.md DOCTRINE).

And "a picture everywhere else" means an app-published representation, not a cached image of the last live frame. Those are different objects with different lifetimes, and the no-screenshot decision above forbids the second one whether it comes from an API or from keeping the last texture around.

5.1 Three things a sign can say, and they are not interchangeable

The first draft wrote *"the sign says what the app accepts and whether it can take work"* as though those were one fact. They are not, and collapsing them is how a road ends up advertising yesterday's capacity.

lifetimewho asserts itmay it show work as transferred
Declared capability — "accepts documents"static; changes only when the manifest changesthe app's manifestno
Reported availability — "two slots free"has an expiry; stale unless refreshedthe app, at runtimeno
Accepted — "this task is yours"one task, one acknowledgementthe coordinatoryes, and only this

Rules that follow:

Measured 2026-09-11 (§12.4a): the split holds under a real handoff. The ledger is empty while an app is working, the road refuses to route "nothing has been ACCEPTED — there is no transfer to route", and what the app receives back from pane_offer is the coordinator's record rather than its own success. Sabotage S10 — let an offer report success without the ledger being written — reddens it.

  • Reported availability carries a freshness stamp and is stale by default. A sign with no

fresh report shows the declared capability and says the availability is unknown — it does not show the last number it heard. Unknown and zero are different signs.

  • The entrance ramp confirms acceptance before it shows a handoff. A ramp that animates on

a reported slot is claiming a transfer that may not have happened, which is §10.9's failure shape — success reported at every layer, with nothing behind it.

  • The sealed arrangement captures the stable half only. §18 of PAPER_ROADS.md seals a

road's arrangement to a sem- id; that seal must cover layout and declared references and must not cover reported availability. Otherwise two identical roads seal differently because one was busier, and the id stops meaning arrangement.

5.2 Discovery belongs to the coordinator, not to the app

Adding 'self' to the CSP makes an app's own fetch('app.json') work, and that is not what §5 claims. "Renderable before any app is live" is not satisfied by the app reading its own sign — that only looks like discovery because the file happens to sit in the same bundle, and nothing about it works for an app that is not installed, not started, or not trusted to describe itself.

The package or the coordinator owns the manifest. The road asks the host, the host holds the package, and no pane need ever have existed.

The durable law is narrower than "the road may not fetch." A first version of the gate banned fetch from the road outright, and that is broader than the architecture: a road may legitimately need unrelated network access later, and a gate that forbids it would be retired the first time it got in the way — taking the real assertion with it. What must hold is that manifest discovery goes through the host-owned package path and cannot silently fall back to a page fetch. tier1-proof asserts exactly that: the sign comes from the host command, no fetch in the road names a manifest or bundle path, there is no catch-and-fetch fallback behind it, and the host is the only reader of the package manifest.

So an entrance sign is a declared accept-clause and an exit ramp is a declared handoff: both render from the coordinator's manifest, not from a running process, and a road can be laid out and sealed before any app is live. What cannot be laid out ahead of time is any claim about capacity — that has an expiry, and it belongs to the coordinator to confirm.

6. Authority — and the inversion nobody should perform by accident

The pane pattern is settled: one capability per pane label, `webviews:` and never `windows:`, generated from the app's manifest, reconciled by `check-webview-acl.mjs`. terminal.json is the worked example and it is three permissions wide.

The trap is which webview is `main`.

Today main is the cockpit and capabilities/default.json grants it twenty-two commands including allow-intent — human-control authority over the runtime. If the road becomes the shell, the road becomes main, and the road would inherit all of it. That is the exact substitution the ACL gate was built to catch, arriving through the front door rather than as a one-word edit.

The road does not need human-control authority. It needs placement and sign rendering. So:

  • the road gets its own, small capability — placement, sign faces, tier transitions;

  • Super's cockpit UI becomes a pane like any other, keeping allow-intent on its own

webviews: ["cockpit"] grant;

  • check-webview-acl.mjs gains one law: **no capability names more than one webview, and

allow-intent names exactly one.**

Stated as a consequence rather than buried: making the road the shell demotes the cockpit from "the trusted surface" to "the surface that happens to hold the runtime grant." That is a better boundary than the one that exists, and it is a change to a boundary, which makes it a ruling and not a refactor.

6.1 A small capability is necessary and not sufficient — the seam is the other half

The capability layer gates which webview may `invoke` which Tauri command. It says nothing about what happens after one of those commands reaches apply(op). If the road can submit an op that a privileged performer executes, the small capability bought nothing: the road did not need cockpit authority, it needed a caller who has it.

So authorization is checked where `apply(op)` executes, against the authenticated caller and its grants — not only at the webview boundary. One shared seam is worth keeping; it does not follow that every caller reaches every op. TABLE stays closed and global; reachability becomes per-actor.

`by` cannot be that caller. ops.js l.174 is apply(op, { by = 'unknown', record: shouldRecord = true } = {}) — `by` is supplied by the caller, defaulted to a string, and exists for the log. Keying authorization on it would be a check you satisfy by writing its argument, which is a defect class this tree has already recorded once. The principal has to arrive from the host side, out of the invoking webview's identity, and the seam has to receive it as something the page cannot set.

The test to add beside the existing seam test:

Can the road request placement while being unable to acquire cockpit authority?

Both halves must be asserted, and the refusal half must be refused by the seam, not by the road's own JavaScript declining to call — the same standard check-webview-acl.mjs already holds for Tauri commands, one layer down.

6.2 The principal — RULED 2026-09-10

The principal is a host-owned identity for a specific pane binding, with explicitly assigned grants, resolved from the injected `Webview` through a host-owned binding registry. A label alone is an identifier, not authority. A request must not be able to supply the authoritative pane label, generation, or grants.

Five consequences, all of them load-bearing:

  1. `by` remains an untrusted log annotation. It stays in the record because a log wants to

know who said it did something. It never reaches an authorization decision.

  1. A webview label identifies a surface; it does not confer authority. The label is how the

host finds the binding. The grants hang off the binding, not off the string.

  1. The host checks authorization before any operation causes a side effect. Not after, not

alongside — a refusal that arrives after the effect is a log entry, not a boundary.

  1. Replacing or unloading a pane revokes its binding, and a delayed operation from a

revoked binding is rejected. This is §10.1's generation requirement arriving from the authority side as well as the liveness side; they are the same fact.

  1. Replaying an operation requires current authorization. A recorded identity carries no

authority. A track is a record of what happened, never a bearer token — which keeps replay honest and stops a recording from being a privilege escalation you can save to disk.

6.2.0 What a request may and may not carry
who supplies itwhy
the surfacethe host, from the injected Webviewthere is no argument to aim elsewhere
the grantsthe host, at bind time, from its own tablea request never mentions them
the pane labelthe host, a constantno command takes a label parameter, and the gate asserts it
the echoed generationthe requestit is compared, never trusted — so it can only cause a refusal, never an elevation, and it is what makes a recorded op detectable as stale (#5)

`authorize` takes `&tauri::Webview`, not `&str`. A string parameter is a check you can satisfy by building its argument — any caller, including one inside the host crate, could pass a label the page chose. Taking the injected webview puts the rule in the type system. Measured consequence: the sabotage that fed by to authorize as the surface no longer compiles. That is the hardening working, and it is also why that sabotage had to be rewritten as a short-circuit before the check — a law with no writable falsifier is untested.

6.2.0a whoami is the hole generation invalidation has, and the label is the fix

whoami takes no echoed generation — it is what a caller uses to learn one. Under a reusable label that is a leak: an instance that outlived its close() calls it, resolves the name to whichever binding now holds it, and comes back carrying the successor's generation. It stops being old.

So a pane's label is its instance: pane-<generation>, and generations only advance, so a label is never reused. An old instance resolves its own revoked binding and is refused; there is no argument it could pass to reach the successor's, because it passes no argument at all. Four rules, and the harness holds all four:

  1. Rebinding destroys the previous instance — and revocation happens first, so a renderer

that outlives its close is already powerless before it could notice.

  1. `whoami` resolves an instance-specific binding, not a reusable label.

  2. The replacement is bound, and its capability minted, before it exists — the capability is

built per instance with CapabilityBuilder at runtime (dynamic-acl), because a static capabilities/pane.json can only name a fixed label.

  1. The previous instance can call nothing, whoami included.

A renderer that survives its own close cannot be summoned on demand (§10.1), so the live battery asserts the structure — the successor is a new instance label — and the registry's unit tests assert the behaviour deterministically, including that a revoked instance offered the successor's generation is refused with PRINCIPAL_REVOKED rather than staleness. One of those tests demonstrates the hole itself on a still-reusable label, so the defence is not merely asserted.

Identity is pulled, not pushed. The first build injected the road's generation with Webview::eval at startup, which races the page's own first script: the road issued its opening op with generation: undefined, was refused, and never finished loading — a blank surface in front of a working host. The repair falls out of the ruling rather than working around it: since the host resolves identity from the injected webview on every call anyway, there was never anything for the page to be told. A grant-free whoami is the bootstrap, and it can name only its own caller.

6.2.1 The implementation check that decides whether any of this is real

If `apply` continues to execute entirely in page JavaScript, adding a principal argument to it establishes nothing. The page can call the performer directly, edit the argument, or skip the seam; a page-side check is advice to itself.

RRABBIT/m2/ops.js is page JavaScript today, and that is the whole difficulty. So the rule this design must hold to:

Either the authoritative check lives in host-controlled code, or every privileged effect passes through a host check. The second is the practical form here.

Which splits the seam into two things that must not be confused:

wherewhat it is forwhat it can enforce
apply(op) — the vocabulary seampageclosed op table, validation, logging, replay, refusal feedbacknothing, against its own page
the host checkRustprincipal → grants → allow/refuse, before the effecteverything

The page-side seam keeps its whole existing job and is still worth having — it is what makes recording, replay and a WRL program one code path. It simply stops being described as a boundary. A privileged op's performer is a Tauri command, and the refusal comes back through the seam rather than being decided by it.

This also settles what an unprivileged op is: one whose entire effect is inside the road's own page (a camera move, a tier the road already owns). Those need no host round trip, and drawing that line is a per-op decision in TABLE, not a global one.

7. What a CD app declares

Do not invent a fourth manifest. The portfolio already has three layers and they compose:

layerfilewhat it says here
[&]*.ampersand.jsonwhat the app composes with — its accept and produce clauses
PULSE*.pulse.jsonits loop: phases, cadence, the tokens it emits and consumes
RuneFort*.rune.jsonhow its pane lays out (runefort.com is a layout protocol for tiled file-backed UIs — its spec dir has no `README.md`; see runefort.protocol.md)

What is genuinely new is small and belongs in one place — call it the road manifest: the entry URL, the sign face, the capability request, the tier policy, and the checkpoint/resume contract from §10.4. Everything else is a reference into the three files above.

Do not claim the road's tiers map onto PULSE's five phase kinds. They do not. PULSE sequences a loop over time; the tier ladder is a residency decision about pixels and processes. CLAUDE.md already records this class of error for the box-and-box rungs, and it is the same error one layer over.

8. What the load balancer actually balances

Not CPU. The shell cannot preempt a webview and should not pretend to.

Three decisions, and keeping them apart is the design:

  1. Placement — which dash on which side. Already solved: nearestFreeSlot for a pane that

was aiming somewhere, nextFreeSlot for a new one.

  1. Residency — which panes hold pixels, which hold a process, which hold nothing. The tier

ladder, driven by view distance and pose. This is the only one with a hard resource behind it, which makes it the only honest use of the word "balancing".

  1. Dispatch — which app gets the next unit of work. A queue keyed by declared accept-clause.

Placement is not scheduling. Moving a pane to another dash must not cancel, pause or reroute its work — and dispatching work to an app must not move its pane. The single most likely way to ruin this design is to let one gesture do both.

9. The signs are certificates, or they are decoration

box-and-box runs feasible ▸ permitted ▸ best over an un-weakenable safety floor, and every verdict ships a certificate (210 enforced property-tested laws + 3 declared-open). That is exactly the ramp decision:

signrungquestion
entrance signalethic / resourcecan this app take this work at all
lane admissiondeonticis it permitted to
exit ramp choiceaxiologicalis it the best of the open ramps
a closed rampany refusalwith a reason printed on the sign

A closed ramp that is a greyed-out button is a UI state. A closed ramp that renders a certificate is a verdict you can argue with, and the second one is the house standard.

10. Traps already measured. This is the durable part of the document.

Each of these cost someone a session already. None is speculative.

10.1 A successful send does not establish that the pane got the message

Measured at D.1.3c·2c·1b·1, restated 2026-09-10 because the first wording was too absolute.

Channel::send does return Result<()> — it is not literally fire-and-forget and it can fail. What it cannot do is confirm receipt: on the non-tracing path it goes Webview::eval → send_user_message (tauri-runtime-wry-2.11.4/src/lib.rs:1854), which posts to the event loop and returns without a getter, so `Ok` is queued-for-a-live-runtime, not received and not processed. Checked against the published docs, which describe the method in one sentence and state no delivery semantics at all.

WebviewEvent carries one variant, `DragDrop`, in 2.11.5 (tauri-2.11.5/src/app.rs:202) — and the enum is #[non_exhaustive], so this is "there is no termination event today", not "there can never be one." Re-check it on a version bump instead of inheriting this sentence.

10.1.1 A real renderer death, measured — and §10.1 holds exactly as written

tier1-proof/tools/renderer-crash.mjs, 12 held · 0 failed. §12.2 only ever exercised a controlled teardown and said so; this kills the pane's renderer outright.

The pane has its own renderer. Under WebKitGTK each webview gets a WebKitWebProcess child of the application: the road alone has one, a promote adds a second. The pane's is identified by the difference between the set before the promote and the set after — no guessing, and the road's own renderer is never touched. That isolation is a Tier 1 result in itself: had the two shared a process, a pane crash would take the shell down.

The timeline, from SIGKILL (the beat interval is 400 ms, the timeout 1500 ms):

+0 … +1200ms   live            the last beat's grace
+1602 … +4027  unresponsive    the clock noticed; it may not say more
+4431          demote          the road acts on a pane it cannot reach
+4834, +5238   gone / absent   NOW it is gone, by a positive fact
+5752          promote         a new instance
+6047 …        live            the replacement, beating

  • The application survives, the road's renderer is untouched, and the road keeps answering

throughout.

  • `unresponsive`, never `gone` for as long as the dead pane is left alone. A clock cannot

pronounce death, and a crash is indistinguishable from a stall by the clock alone — which is the whole of §10.1 and is exactly what a design must not paper over.

  • `present` stays true the entire time. Tauri still holds the webview; there is no destroyed

event to hear. The webview is a live object with nothing behind it.

  • WebKitGTK does not respawn it. Nothing recovers the pane except the host.

  • Recovery works: demote a pane whose renderer is dead, then promote a fresh instance.

Two things the probe had to be built around.

A renderer crash DELETES THE WEBDRIVER SESSION — the next command returns invalid session id: session deleted because of page crash or hang. The crash cannot be watched through the channel that set it up, and the first version of the probe died at exactly that line. So the road records the timeline into its own localStorage and a later session reads it back; and because WebDriver is gone, the road also drives its own recovery, being the only thing left that can still reach the host. Nothing was added to the product to make that work.

Both of the probe's own bugs were assertion WINDOWS, the same class as the geometry check sampled before layout had settled: counting the demote's own correct gone as a violation of the rule it obeys, and reading the renderer count at the end, where the replacement pane's renderer looks exactly like the dead one coming back.

What follows for the design:

  • Generation + acknowledgement is the mechanism. A bind arriving while a presentation is

open is a positive fact that the old renderer is gone. Acknowledgements make delivery observable where Ok does not.

  • A missed heartbeat means `unresponsive` or `unknown` — never `dead`. Sleep, throttling, a

busy main thread and a backgrounded display all resemble failure. Only a positive fact (a new bind, an explicit close, an exited process) may move a pane to gone.

  • An old-generation message must never regain control of a replacement pane. Every message

carries its generation, the host drops any that is not current, and a re-bind invalidates the previous one. Without this, a slow reply from a dead renderer lands in its successor — the worst failure available here, because both ends report success.

10.2 The road canvas and the pane will fight over the pointer, in both directions

PAPER_ROADS.md §21.2 measured that Chrome's elementFromPoint over a mounted read pane returns CANVAS#gl — the canvas swallows clicks meant for the DOM. A live OS webview inverts it: the webview is composited above the entire page, so it swallows clicks meant for the road, and no elementFromPoint reaches across the boundary at all.

Therefore `unread` must never depend on a click landing on the road behind a live pane. Esc already lives in the capture chain for exactly this reason — and PAPER_ROADS.md DOCTRINE records that lesson being written down in `TRACKS_HANDOFF.md` §3 and then repeated anyway.

10.3 Focus has never been routed, and the conformance suite has never been keyed

§21.4: Tab then Return inside a read pane produced last: null — openRead focuses [tabindex="0"], a[href], h1 and a BendScript title h1 takes no focus. Worse, stated there in full: "The spec-conformance suite and the running pane have never been checked against each other with a keyboard." A live pane makes focus routing mandatory rather than cosmetic.

10.4 Hiding a webview is not pausing it, and there is no portable primitive that is

hide() removes a webview from view. It does not stop its timers, release its process, or checkpoint its state. macOS suspension behaviour is documented for app backgrounding, not for a hidden webview in a foreground app, and the one preference in that area (WKSuspendInBackground) is not a per-pane control.

So the shell's only hard lever is destroy. Anything softer must be cooperative: the app implements checkpoint/resume, or a resident tier is a claim the shell cannot keep. This is why §4's table stops at live.

10.5 rest / wake already mean something else

ops.js l.120–121: they park and wake an agent, setting WRL Core §20.1's quiescent/runnable (m2/mail/box.js). Reusing them for pane residency would conflate an agent's liveness with a surface's. Either new op names, or a ruling that says the two are the same thing. They are not obviously the same thing.

10.6 On Linux, adding a child webview COLLAPSES THE PARENT — measured, and worse than reported

preview.rs carries the known form: "Tauri's Linux child WebViews are packed in a vertical GtkBox; their set_position/set_size methods do not position them inside the cockpit." Upstream #13071 confirms it is Linux-specific, and the fix in the tree is a GTK overlay that preserves the IPC label.

That undersells it. Measured 2026-09-10 by tier1-proof/tools/geometry-probe.mjs, on the harness with the workaround deliberately not ported (WebKitGTK, dpr 2):

requested read rectx=315 y=93 522 × 262
road before promote1000 × 653
pane after promote1000 × 653 — the requested rect ignored entirely
road after promote1000 × 1

The child takes the whole window and the road collapses to one pixel. It is not that the pane sits in the wrong place; the road stops having a surface. Any road shell on Linux needs the overlay from the first pane, not as a polish pass — and a session that skips it will see the road vanish and reach for a rendering bug.

10.6.1 CLOSED on Linux — and it took two GTK facts, both measured

tier1-proof/src/layout.rs ports the overlay from super/cockpit/src/preview.rs: the road is moved into a GtkOverlay once, and every pane is an overlay child. Result: road 1000 × 653, pane 522 × 262 — the requested rect exactly. Two things the port had to learn that the cockpit does not need, because its pane is meant to fill the area it is given and ours is a read pose of a stated size:

  • `set_size_request` is a MINIMUM, and a WebKitWebView's natural size exceeds it. With

alignment and margins alone the pane ran from its margin to the far edge: requested 522 × 262 at (315, 93), allocated 685 × 560 = (1000−315) × (653−93). Turning hexpand/vexpand off did not change it. get-child-position is the only place in GTK3 that states an overlay child's allocation outright, so the read pose is expressed there.

  • Margins are applied INSIDE the allocation you return, so they are subtracted twice.

Returning (margin_start, margin_top, size_request) produced 207 × 169, and 522−315 = 207, 262−93 = 169. The numbers name the defect. The position belongs in the returned rectangle; the margins are zero.

10.6.2 The read pose is reached ASYNCHRONOUSLY, and that is a design fact

Measured: the pane is created at full window size and GTK re-allocates it afterwards — ~2.8 s to settle in this harness. A check made the instant promote returns reads 1000 × 653; a check after settling reads 522 × 262. Both are true and only one is the claim.

A road that draws its own chrome will see that first frame. The window is named here rather than slept through, and the battery's assertion carries its deadline in its own name.

The corollary bit twice. Sabotage S5 removes the layout call, and the road assertion passed under it while measured immediately after promote, because the road is still full-size for the moment before GTK re-allocates. It survived only because the pane assertion failed beside it. A geometry assertion made before layout has settled is not a geometry assertion; both are now measured after the pane settles, and S5 reddens both.

10.6.3 Eventual geometry is not containment

The asynchronous pose was first reported as a timing note. It is a containment defect. For those ~2.8 s an untrusted pane covered the entire road and took input over all of it, while every post-settle assertion passed. A gate that only checks the end state cannot see this at all.

The rule: a pane is neither visible nor interactive until its allocation is the read pose, and then it becomes both at once. In tier1-proof that is opacity 0 plus insensitive — not hidden, because a GTK widget that has never been shown is never laid out, so hiding it would mean waiting for an allocation that can never arrive. layout::reveal is the only thing that undoes either, and it does both together.

A pose that never arrives abandons the promote. The pane is never shown late and never shown wrong; a promote that cannot reach the pose closes the child and revokes its binding.

Measured after the change: 73 samples across the transition, none of them visible or interactive outside the rectangle; the host held the pane contained for 2709 ms and then revealed it; and the post-reveal pose settles in 7 ms rather than 2782, because by then it is already correct.

The test samples from creation through settling, not at the end — promote is started without being awaited and the host is polled while it runs. Two sabotages target this (S5, S7) and both redden it.

10.6.4 A synchronous Tauri command runs on the main thread

The containment loop did not work at first, and the reason is worth more than the fix.

A synchronous #[tauri::command] runs on the main thread. A command that waits for GTK to allocate is therefore blocking the layout pass it is waiting for: measured, the overlay sat at GTK's never-allocated sentinel (-1,-1,1,1) inside a box that was already 1000 × 653, for the full five-second deadline, every time. queue_resize on the container did not help and could not — nothing was going to run it.

The symptom is maximally misleading: every instrument answers. with_webview executes inline when it is already on the main thread, so place succeeded and allocation returned real values. The only thing that never happened was the layout. async fn is the fix, and super/cockpit's browser_surface is async for the same reason from the other side.

Any host-side "wait until the platform has done something" must be async. That is a rule about the road shell, not about this harness.

10.6.5 The pane's on-screen POSITION, measured from outside the process

Size was asserted from the start and position was not, because neither instrument can answer it: the battery reads the pane's own innerWidth, which says nothing about where the pane sits, and the host's allocation reports x/y as 0,0 because a WebKitWebView has its own GdkWindow and its allocation is relative to that. So the question was left open and named as open.

tier1-proof/tools/pose-screenshot.mjs answers it in pixels:

requested   522 × 262 at (315, 93) CSS   ·   device pixel ratio 2
expected    1044 × 524 at (630, 186) device px
measured    1044x524+630+186
delta       x 0 · y 0 · w 0 · h 0

A difference of two captures is not the measurement, and trying it first is what showed why. Clicking read also hides the sign and rewrites the status block, so the changed region came back 1915x1386 — essentially the whole window. The pane has to identify itself: it paints one colour that appears nowhere else on the road, over its whole viewport, and the bounding box of that colour in a capture of the window is the rectangle, independent of what either page chose to draw. docs/tier1-read-pose-probe.png is that frame; docs/tier1-read-pose.png is what a person sees. In both, the road's amber centre line resumes on either side of the pane — an independent check on the left and right edges.

Two capture-path caveats, because the picture is only as good as how it was taken. This box is GNOME on Wayland: there is no grim (wlroots only) and GNOME's own capture is a portal that wants a human, so the app is launched with GDK_BACKEND=x11 and captured through XWayland. The GtkOverlay layout being measured is backend-independent — it is the same get-child-position either way — but the capture path is not the shipping one. And import -window root fails outright here ("missing an image filename"), as does the -window <title> form; the window id from _NET_CLIENT_LIST plus a WM_NAME match is what works.

This probe does not run in CI — it needs a real display, an X server and ImageMagick — so it is a bench instrument, not a gate.

The same probe is the macOS test. On NSView subviews the prediction is the parent stays 1000 × 653 and the child is 522 × 262. One command, and §11 stops being a hypothesis on this axis. Until it is run, it has not been run.

10.7 The UI is baked into the binary

tauri.conf.json has "frontendDist": "ui", so generate_context! embeds the bytes. Editing cockpit/ui/*.js and re-running changes nothing. Cost one full battery run against a file that plainly defined the missing function. Always `cargo build --release` after touching the UI. For a road whose panes are separate dev servers this will bite twice as often.

10.8 The multiwebview API is unstable, and its open bugs are the ones this design leans on

Resize stops working after repeated window resizes (#10131), positioning is lost across maximize/restore (#11170), the four-corner example stacks vertically (#10420). A road that repositions panes every frame is the worst case for all three. Budget for them; do not discover them.

10.9 An op that reports success at every step and shows nothing

§17.1 — casting a pane returned ok at three layers while the screen stayed on the default panel. "Three separate layers each answered 'yes' about a thing none of them could show." A pane that reports live is worth exactly nothing until something reads the rect.

11. macOS

macOS is an EXPLICITLY UNVERIFIED TARGET. There is no Mac here, nothing in this section has been run on one, and development continues on Linux without waiting. The first draft said "macOS is the easier side"; one deleted workaround does not establish that, and the section is written as a claim to be falsified rather than a plan.

The Mac runtime check is a RELEASE GATE, not a development blocker. Nothing downstream waits on it; a release that claims macOS support does. tier1-proof/tools/geometry-probe.mjs is that gate in one command, and it is deliberately portable so the machine can be borrowed or hosted — any Apple Silicon Mac that runs the chosen minimum macOS version settles it, and a hosted interactive Mac settles it before anyone buys one.

CI compiles on macOS and that is ALL it proves. tier1-proof/.github/workflows/ runs cargo build + cargo test on macos-14, which catches platform compilation problems — the cfg-gated layout.rs branch, a diverging tauri API, a dependency that does not build. It cannot validate WKWebView geometry, the read pose, containment, or input reaching a pane: those need a real display and a real webview. The job prints that limit as a warning on every run, because a green tick that reads as "macOS works" is worse than no job.

The hypothesis: Tier 1 ports to macOS with no new mechanism, and the Linux-specific positioning workaround is removed rather than replaced.

What supports it:

  • Tauri targets macOS natively; the webview is WKWebView via wry.

  • §10.6's GTK overlay exists because Tauri's Linux child webviews are packed in a vertical

GtkBox and ignore set_position; upstream (#13071) confirms it is Linux-specific and macOS uses NSView subviews. This is the one piece of evidence, and it is about one axis.

  • No transparency is required. A road inside an ordinary window avoids macOSPrivateApi

entirely — which matters, because transparency on macOS has historically required it (and that disqualifies App Store submission), with an open bug where it is lost after a DMG build (#13415).

  • Signing and notarization are a documented path.

The geometry contract, stated so it is portable. On Linux, with the overlay: parent stays 1000 × 653, child is 522 × 262 at the requested rect, and no sample is visible or interactive outside that rectangle at any point in the transition. The macOS prediction is the same three, reached without the overlay because a child webview is an ordinary NSView subview. Either the numbers come back or they do not.

What must be measured before the hypothesis is accepted — none of these can be argued from Linux, and each has been a real source of divergence in WKWebView:

why it is on the list
focus§10.3 — focus routing has never been built on either platform, and WKWebView's first-responder rules are its own
typing / IMEa live pane is the first surface here that takes text
resize#10131 and #11170 are the multiwebview resize and maximize/restore bugs
display scalingbacking-scale and the scale_factor the rect maths in preview.rs already depends on
storagesee the caveat below
recovery§10.1's generation + heartbeat, against a real WKWebView termination
containment§10.6.3 — whether a child NSView is ever composited before its frame is set
threading§10.6.4 — whether a sync command blocks layout there too

Storage — a correction to the first draft. dataStoreIdentifier on WebviewBuilder is macOS 14+ and iOS 17+, and unsupported on Windows, Linux and Android. It initialises a WKWebsiteDataStore with a UUID so cookies and website data land in a per-identifier directory rather than the shared one. That is website-data separation, not per-pane security isolation — it is not a sandbox, not a process boundary, and not a substitute for the capability work in §6. Describing it as isolation was an overstatement.

Frame rate is a measurement, not a headline. There are reports of a 60 fps cap on macOS with ProMotion reachable only through a private-API plugin, and WebKitGTK separately masks its renderer string and can hand back a software rasterizer without saying so. Both are reasons to measure this scene — 1,386 scene objects and 24 canvases at the ten-thousand-document rung (PAPER_ROADS.md §15) — not to name a principal risk in advance.

Not in scope, by the ruling: other applications' Mac windows. That was Tier 3 and it is closed.

iPad is a different product. Tauri v2 does build for iOS, multiwebview is unstable there, and iPadOS has no free window placement. One road, one pane, or don't.

12. The one narrow proof — BUILT AND GREEN, 2026-09-10

`RRABBIT/tier1-proof/` — 28 held · 0 failed live, 18 held · 0 failed static, 4 registry unit tests, and seven sabotages — every one a falsifier.

The first report of this said 23 · 0 with geometry listed as "not measured", and that was the wrong shape. Geometry is half the central promise — a road that collapses to one pixel when a pane goes live has not performed the transition, whatever the authority assertions say. The read pose is an acceptance gate now (§12.1, 2b), not a diagnostic beside one, and the geometry-probe remains only as the platform instrument and the macOS contract.

The rest of this section is what it was specified to do; §12.6 is what it actually found.

Build exactly one transition and nothing else:

published sign  →  read pose  →  LIVE pane  →  leave read pose  →  published sign
                                     │
                              state preserved
                          stale messages rejected

This is the central claim of the whole document. Everything in §§4–9 is arranged around the promotion and demotion of a single pane, so if that round trip is not sound, the remaining decisions would accumulate on top of an unproven transition — which is the reason to build this first rather than the manifest, the dispatch queue, or a second pane.

12.1 What the proof must assert

Nine assertions. A screenshot is not one of them — §10.9 records three layers reporting success over a screen showing nothing, and this transition has exactly that shape.

#assertionfails if
1the sign renders from the published representation, with no live pane in existenceanything reads a texture or a snapshot
2read promotes exactly one pane to live; the child webview exists at the read rectthe rect is wrong, or two are live (§4.1)
3pointer and keyboard reach the pane while live§10.2 — the road canvas is still taking the clicks
4unread demotes: the webview is destroyed and the published sign is backthe last frame is kept as the picture (§5)
5state survives the round trip, via the app's checkpoint/resume — not via the shellthe shell is holding the app's state for it (§10.4)
6every host→pane message carries a generation; the pane rejects any that is not currenta stale message is accepted
7after demote+promote, a message from the old generation is dropped by the host§10.1 — a dead renderer's reply lands in its successor
8a missed heartbeat reports unresponsive, and only a positive fact reports gonea sleeping pane is declared dead
9athe road successfully performs an allowed placement opthe allowed half is untested and 9b proves only that nothing works
9bthe host refuses a privileged op from the road even when the request claims `by: 'cockpit'`by reached a decision, or our JavaScript declined instead of the host refusing
9cafter re-binding, a captured old-generation request is rejected§6.2 #4 — a revoked binding still acts

12.1a Seven sabotages, and the accident that happened twice

A botched edit injected two sabotages into the harness by accident — an authority bypass and a skipped layout call. The static gate caught the authority one before any test ran. Nothing static could catch the other; only the live geometry assertion found it. Then the identical accident happened a second time, and again geometry was the only thing that noticed. Twice is not a coincidence and it is the argument for the promotion, made by accident and kept.

S5's law moved, and the sweep is what said so. It used to break "the road collapses to one pixel"; once the pane is contained until its allocation is correct, skipping the layout means the pose never arrives and the promote is abandoned, so the road never sees a collapsed surface at all. The reporter called it red, but not on the named law, which is exactly what that outcome is for — the sabotage still bites, on a different assertion, and the law it was named for is now unreachable from outside.

12.2 The sabotage each assertion owes

The cockpit's own standard, applied here: an assertion that cannot be made to fail has not been tested. Each sabotage below states which failure it actually exercises, because two of them were originally one and the pair do not test the same thing.

sabotageexercisesmust read
delay a heartbeat past the timeouta slow or throttled paneunresponsive, never gone
replay a captured old-generation request after a re-promotea revoked binding (§6.2 #4)rejected by the host
forge by: 'cockpit' on a privileged op from the roadby reaching a decisionrefused by the host
kill the pane's dev server while livesource availability onlythe road must not upgrade this to gone
terminate the renderer / tear the pane down under controlrenderer deathgone, by a positive fact
flip the pane's capability to windows:the ACL gatecheck-webview-acl.mjs red

The dev-server kill and the renderer termination are different tests and the first was mislabelled. An already-loaded page keeps running with its origin gone: nothing is fetched, so nothing fails, and a pane that never reloads may be perfectly healthy for hours. Treating that as death would make every restarted dev server look like a crash. It is kept — it is a real condition the road must not over-read — but the renderer-death assertion needs its own, positive-fact test beside it.

12.3 Where it is built, and why not in the cockpit

In its own harness, not by re-rooting `super/cockpit/`. §13 #1 — whether the road becomes main and demotes the cockpit — is unruled, and re-rooting the cockpit to run this proof would answer it by accident, which is precisely the front-door inheritance §6 warns about. A standalone harness proves the transition without touching the boundary, and the ruling stays open until it is made deliberately.

12.3a What the build settled

  • `tauri::Webview` is injectable as a command argument, so the principal really is derived

by the host from the actual invoking webview. That is the mechanism §6.2 needs and it is confirmed by the compiler, not by reading docs.

  • The ACL layer and the seam are independently observable. capabilities/road.json grants

allow-privileged-intent to the road on purpose; the road invokes it and the host refuses with PRINCIPAL_GRANT_NOT_HELD. An assertion checks the refusal is not tauri's resolver, so the two layers cannot be confused for one another.

  • `N = 1` is enforced where it can refuse, not where it is convenient: a second promote

returns TIER_ALREADY_LIVE from the host.

  • `gone` never comes from a clock. liveness takes the caller's measured present fact;

the timeout can only produce unresponsive. Sabotage S3 makes the clock say gone and the battery reddens.

12.4 Then, and only then

  1. The manifest and a second pane (§7), with two capabilities generated rather than

hand-written and §6's one-webview law added to the gate.

  1. The seam-authorization test from §6.1 — *can the road request placement while being unable

to acquire cockpit authority?*

  1. The same nine assertions on a Mac, plus §11's six-row measurement table, before anything

is built on top of the Mac result.

12.4a The second proof — TWO APPS, ONE LIVE PANE, built 2026-09-11

`tier1-proof/tools/handoff-battery.mjs` — 21 held · 0 failed.

The first proof answered whether a pane can stand on a road at all. This one asks whether the rules compose across an app boundary, which is where they are first able to contradict each other. Two packages in the coordinator's catalogue: notes (accepts document, produces summary) and digest (accepts summary, produces nothing).

`N = 1` was not a blocker for this, and assuming it would have been is worth naming. The budget limits simultaneous live panes; two apps, routing, eviction, state and sequential promotion are all provable under it. Only simultaneous residency needs §13 #6. Likewise §5's claim is strongest with zero live panes, not one.

What it establishes:

both signs render with zero live panesthe catalogue is the coordinator's; nothing started to draw a road
routing reads the DECLARATIONdocument→notes, summary→digest, and an unroutable kind is refused NO_ROUTE by name, not dropped
an app's report is not a transferthe ledger is empty until the coordinator accepts, and the road has nothing to route until then
acceptance is a RECORDwhat the app gets back is the coordinator's ledger entry, not its own claim
eviction is how the second app standsevict → route the accepted kind → promote the next, a genuinely different instance
authority does not cross the boundarydigest declares no produces, is never granted offer, and is refused by the host when it tries
state survives evictionboth apps restore their exact state using package-prefixed keys; the shared origin does not isolate their storage
at most one live pane at every observationsampled across the handoff and both restorations

A grant derived from a declaration is the part worth keeping. packages::grants_for reads the manifest's produces and grants offer only where something is produced, and the instance capability mirrors it. So "what this app may do" is a consequence of what it said it was, checked by the host — not a role handed out by the shell.

The terminal refusal is defended at three layers, and the sabotage that falsifies it has to dismantle all three — the grant table, the instance capability, and the declaration check in pane_offer. A sabotage needing three edits is evidence the layers are not one layer written three times.

12.4b The actual road seam crosses the native boundary — 2026-09-12

The harness's own table was not evidence about m2/ops.js: the actual road seam treated a Promise as immediate success, recorded it before host acceptance, and replayed subsequent steps before the host replied. test/ops-async.mjs exercises that failure against the previous implementation (nine tests fail there).

apply, replay, and precheck now preserve their synchronous result for existing performers and return a Promise of that same result when work is asynchronous. Only successful completion reaches the log. Host refusal codes survive; rejected performers become OP_THREW. Replay waits for each step and stops on refusal. Reset fences late completion from the next world's log and stops old replay, but cannot undo a host effect already started. Independent calls must be sequenced by their caller; this is not a global task scheduler.

tier1-proof/tools/road-seam-battery.mjs executes the actual module against Tauri with a small read/unread adapter. It measures native placement, revocation, stale identity refusal, successful-only recording, program use, and replay of the recorded plan. Because that plan omits unread, read supersedes an existing pane before promotion, preserving both the paper semantics and N=1. No op names are added.

Updated 2026-09-12: the shared Tauri road now has a Three.js scene, published sign textures, entrance/exit gantries, forward travel and front-normal camera arrival. The projected sign and native read frame were measured coincident at 2× fullscreen scale, with no native pane present during approach. Leaving destroys the pane and returns to the saved lane position. This is the shared Tauri surface's visual controller, not a replacement for the m2 compositor. The m2 operation adapter remains the independent seam proof described above. The subsequent two-lane pass adds Documents/Notes and Summaries/Digest with paved connecting ramps. Camera and pavement use the same curve; an accepted handoff travels to the destination lane before promotion. These are fixed presentation lanes, not Super runtime work lanes. The full cockpit and Super task routing remain unfinished; simultaneous native residency remains N=1.

12.5 What would falsify the whole approach

A consumer that needs a special case at the seam. That is OP_VOCABULARY_DRAFT.md §9's test; it passed with three consumers, and a road shell is the fourth. If placing and tiering a live pane cannot go through apply, the seam is wrong and this document is wrong with it.

12.6 Traps the build paid for, and two of them are about the design

A CSP that names `connect-src` for IPC blocks an app from fetching its own manifest. connect-src ipc: http://ipc.localhost — copied from the cockpit, where it is correct — excludes 'self', so fetch('app.json') throws TypeError: Load failed. The symptom is a page that never becomes ready with nothing in the console, while window.__TAURI__ and the host-injected generation are both fine, which reads exactly like a load-order bug. This one is not incidental to the harness: §5 makes every CD app's sign a fetched manifest, so the road shell would have met it on its first app.

A battery that is not idempotent reports its previous run. WebDriver's /value appends, and the pane's localStorage outlives the application, so the second run typed into an already full field. It was invisible while the suite was green — the sabotage sweep is what exposed it, because four sabotages each reddened two assertions they do not touch. Collateral damage in a sabotage is a defect in the instrument, and the sweep is the only thing that shows it.

Restoring the source is not restoring the artifact. sabotage.sh put the source back and did not rebuild, so the next battery run measured the sabotaged binary and reported two refusals that had already been fixed. Same class as §10.7 — frontendDist bakes the UI in — and the rule is the same: `cargo build --release` after every change, including after an undo.

A `str.replace` that matches nothing still prints success. Two edits in this build reported themselves done and had changed nothing: the CSP revert, and a batch of tool edits lost to a quoting error. One of them I then stated as fact in a message. Every replacement asserts its anchor now, and the static gate is what caught the CSP claim rather than any reading of it.

A sweep that greps for a named failure must distinguish "green" from "red elsewhere." The first version printed "the battery stayed green over a broken law" whenever its pattern missed — and it missed on two sabotages that had reddened the battery, just not on the line the pattern named. A sweep that reports a red run as green retires a law that is in fact tested. Three outcomes now: falsifier, red-but-not-on-the-named-law, or genuinely green.

13. [TRAVIS] decisions this document does not make

  1. Does the road become `main`, demoting the cockpit to a pane? (§6. It is a boundary

change, so it is a ruling.)

  1. **New op names for tier transitions, or is a pane's residency the same fact as an agent's

quiescent/runnable?** (§10.5.)

  1. Is the road manifest a fourth file, or a section inside the [&] manifest? (§7.)

  2. **Does the op vocabulary ruling in OP_VOCABULARY_DRAFT.md §8 now cover a program as an

actor?** Every consumer so far has been a human, a replay, or a WRL script inside the shell. A CD app dispatching work through the seam is the first actor outside it.

  1. ~~What is the authenticated principal at the seam?~~ RULED 2026-09-10 — see §6.2.

A host-owned identity for a specific pane binding, with explicitly assigned grants, derived by the host from the invoking webview and its current binding generation; the page can supply neither. The consequence that reshapes the build is §6.2.1: a page-side apply cannot enforce this, so every privileged effect passes through a host check.

  1. Is the live budget `N = 1`? (§4.1 proposes it for v1. Raising it is a resource ruling

against a measurement, not a rendering change.)

  1. May a live pane load an external origin? preview.rs allows it with on_navigation;

a CD app arguably should be served from a custom URI scheme (register_asynchronous_uri_scheme_protocol) instead. These are different threat models.

Publish the coordinator's package and task before creating the child; clear them if creation or placement fails. Waiting until reveal races pane_hello.

  • measured — the Tauri host, the multi-webview primitive, the external-URL child webview

with a navigation policy, and the per-webview ACL gate all exist in super/cockpit/ today. The primitive is not a proposal; Cargo.toml:17 turns it on and says why.

  • found — an OS child webview is an axis-aligned rectangle and cannot be drawn into a

three.js scene. The existing read pose already resolves it: live only in the read pose, a picture everywhere else. No new navigation verb is required.

  • proposed — a fourth tier, live, above hidden/card/paint. What would test it: §12.

  • corrected — "live is bounded by pose, not by policy" was wrong, and cast already

falsifies it: an on-air pane pins its paint tier and outlives its pose on purpose (PAPER_ROADS.md §17.1). Pose eligibility is not a resource budget. The budget is a separate rule — how many, when unloaded, how state survives — and v1 is N = 1.

  • corrected — "what the app accepts and whether it can take work" was one sentence over

two facts with different lifetimes. Declared / reported-with-an-expiry / accepted are three things; only the coordinator's acceptance may show work as transferred, and only the declared half may enter the sealed arrangement.

  • found — a small road capability gates invoke and nothing downstream of it. **The seam is

the other half of the boundary**, and by cannot be the principal: ops.js l.174 lets the caller supply it. A check you satisfy by writing its argument is not a check.

  • ruled (Travis, 2026-09-10, §6.2) — the principal is a **host-owned identity for a pane

binding, derived from the invoking webview and its current generation, with grants the page can neither supply nor override. `by` stays an untrusted log annotation; a label identifies a surface and confers nothing; revoking a binding rejects its delayed operations; and a recorded identity carries no authority**, so replay needs current authorization.

  • found — the ruling does not survive a page-side seam. ops.js is page JavaScript, and a

principal argument added to it is advice a page gives itself. The vocabulary seam (page) and the authority check (host) are two things; the first keeps its whole job and stops being called a boundary.

  • corrected — "kill the pane's dev server" was labelled a renderer-death test and is not

one: an already-loaded page keeps running with its origin gone. It exercises source availability, and renderer death needs its own positive-fact test beside it.

  • found — making the road main would hand it the cockpit's twenty-two-command grant,

including allow-intent, through the front door. The gate that exists catches the one-word edit and would not catch this.

  • corrected — "Channel::send is fire-and-forget" was too absolute. It returns

Result<()> and can fail; what it cannot do is establish receipt or processing, because the non-tracing path posts to the event loop without a getter. And WebviewEvent is #[non_exhaustive] — one variant today (2.11.5), not one variant forever. Re-check on a version bump.

  • found — a missed heartbeat is unresponsive or unknown, never gone; sleep and

throttling resemble failure. And an old-generation message must never reach a replacement pane — that is the failure where both ends report success.

  • measured — no wry or core-Tauri webview snapshot API exists. **The sign face is published

by the app, not sampled from it** — which is also the answer that makes an advert an advert.

  • found — hiding a webview is not pausing it and there is no portable primitive that is.

The shell's only hard lever is destroy; anything softer is a cooperative contract.

  • found — rest/wake are already an agent's quiescent/runnable. Reusing them for pane

residency conflates two different livenesses.

  • hypothesis, not finding — "macOS is the easier side." One deleted Linux workaround is

evidence about one axis. Focus, typing/IME, resize, display scaling, storage and recovery are unmeasured, and §11 is written as a claim to falsify.

  • corrected — dataStoreIdentifier is macOS 14+ / iOS 17+, unsupported elsewhere, and

it separates website data, not processes. Calling it per-pane security isolation was an overstatement; it is not a substitute for §6.

  • proposed — placement, residency and dispatch are three decisions and only residency has a

hard resource behind it. What would test it: a gesture that moves a pane must leave its queue position unchanged, and a dispatch must leave its dash unchanged.

  • not measured — what the 3D road costs in WKWebView, whether the reported 60 fps cap binds

it, and how many live panes a Mac tolerates. All three are first-week measurements and none of them can be argued from here. The reported cap is not promoted to the principal Mac risk until this scene is measured.

  • measured — §12's round trip is built and green: RRABBIT/tier1-proof/, **28 held · 0

failed live, static gate 18 held · 0 failed**, 4 registry unit tests, seven sabotages, every one a falsifier. Sign published by the coordinator (not sampled, not fetched by the app), one live pane at the requested rect with the road intact, real clicks and keys into it, app state surviving destroy+recreate with the host holding no copy, and every stale generation refused by the host in both directions.

  • corrected — the first report called that green while geometry was failing. **Geometry is

half the central promise, so it is an acceptance gate, not a diagnostic.** A road that collapses to one pixel has not entered the read pose whatever the authority suite says.

  • corrected, again — the asynchronous pose was reported as a timing note and it is a

containment defect: for ~2.8 s an untrusted pane covered the whole road and took input over all of it while every post-settle assertion passed. Eventual geometry is not containment. A pane is now neither visible nor interactive until its allocation is the read pose, and then both at once; a pose that never arrives abandons the promote. Measured: 73 samples across the transition, none outside the rectangle; 2709 ms contained; 7 ms to settle after reveal, because by then it is already correct.

  • found — contained means opacity 0 plus insensitive, not hidden: a GTK widget that has

never been shown is never laid out, so hiding it means waiting for an allocation that cannot arrive.

  • found — a synchronous `#[tauri::command]` runs on the main thread, so a command that

waits for the platform blocks the very work it waits for. Measured: the overlay sat at GTK's never-allocated sentinel for the full deadline while place and allocation both succeeded — with_webview runs inline when already on the main thread, so every instrument answered and only the layout never happened. Any host-side wait must be async.

  • found — `whoami` is the hole generation invalidation has. It takes no echoed

generation, so under a reusable label an instance that outlived its close could call it and come back carrying the successor's. A pane's label is now its instance, pane-<generation>, with the capability minted per instance at runtime; a static capability file cannot express this because it names a fixed label.

  • corrected — banning fetch from the road outright was broader than the law and would

have been retired the first time a road needed unrelated network access, taking the real assertion with it. What is asserted now: manifest discovery goes through the host-owned package path and cannot silently fall back to a page fetch.

  • measured — §10.6 is CLOSED on Linux: road 1000 × 653, pane 522 × 262. It took two GTK

facts, both of which the cockpit's port does not need — set_size_request is a minimum a WebKitWebView's natural size exceeds (685 × 560), and margins are subtracted a second time inside the allocation you return (207 × 169 = 522−315 by 262−93).

  • found — the read pose is reached asynchronously, ~2.8 s here, full-window at first

paint. A road drawing its own chrome will see that frame. And a geometry assertion made before layout settles is not one: measured early, the road check passed under the sabotage that removes the layout call.

  • found — pushing identity into a page RACES its first script. eval at startup left the

road issuing its opening op with generation: undefined. Pull, not push — and it falls out of §6.2, since the host resolves identity per call anyway.

  • found — authorize taking &tauri::Webview rather than &str made one sabotage

uncompilable. Hardening working; and a law with no writable falsifier is untested, so the sabotage moved to a short-circuit before the check.

  • found — an accidental edit injected two sabotages at once. The static gate caught the

authority one before any test ran; nothing static could catch the geometry one.

  • measured — tauri::Webview is injectable as a command argument, so the principal is

genuinely host-derived from the invoking webview. §6.2 has a mechanism, not just a rule.

  • found — a CSP naming connect-src for IPC **blocks the app from fetching its own

manifest**, and fails as a page that never becomes ready with an empty console. §5 makes every CD app sign a fetched manifest, so this is the road shell's trap and not the harness's.

  • found — a green suite proves nothing about its own idempotence. /value appends and

localStorage outlives the app; the sabotage sweep exposed it by reddening assertions the sabotages do not touch. Collateral in a sweep is a defect in the instrument.

  • found, again — restoring source is not restoring the artifact. The sweep left the

sabotaged binary in target/release and the next run measured it. §10.7, one directory over.

  • measured, and worse than the tree recorded — on Linux add_child gives the child the

WHOLE window and collapses the parent to 1000 × 1: the road stops having a surface, rather than merely sitting behind a mis-placed pane. §10.6 has the numbers; tier1-proof/tools/geometry-probe.mjs is the instrument, and it is also the macOS test — the prediction there is parent 1000 × 653, child 522 × 262.

  • found — the authority suite stayed 23/23 green through that, because it asserts nothing

about geometry. That is the separation working: a platform defect must not be able to redden an authority battery, and it did not.

  • measured, from outside the process — the pane's on-screen POSITION, which was previously

named as unverified: 1044x524+630+186 against an expected 1044 × 524 at (630, 186), delta 0 on all four. A two-capture difference is NOT the measurement — clicking read also hides the sign and rewrites the status block, so the changed region came back 1915x1386. The pane identifies itself by painting a colour that appears nowhere else, and the bounding box of that colour is the rectangle. Pictures in docs/tier1-read-pose.png and docs/tier1-read-pose-probe.png.

  • stated as a limit — that capture goes through XWayland (GDK_BACKEND=x11), because

this box is GNOME/Wayland with no grim and a portal that wants a human. The layout measured is backend-independent; the capture path is not the shipping one. import -window root and -window <title> both fail here — the window id from _NET_CLIENT_LIST is what works. The probe needs a display and ImageMagick, so it is a bench instrument and not a gate.

  • measured — an actual renderer death, SIGKILL to the pane's own WebKitWebProcess:

§10.1 holds exactly as written. unresponsive and never gone while the dead pane is left alone, present true throughout, the road untouched and still answering, WebKitGTK does not respawn it, and demote-then-promote recovers into a new instance. §10.1.1 has the timeline.

  • found — a renderer crash deletes the WebDriver session, so the crash cannot be observed

through the channel that set it up. The road records to its own storage and drives its own recovery; a later session reads it back.

  • found, a third time — both of that probe's bugs were assertion WINDOWS. A window that

extends past a deliberate act counts that act as a violation of the rule it obeys.

  • blocked on a ruling, not on effort — source unavailability. The harness bakes its UI into

the binary, so there is no origin to take away; reaching the condition needs a pane on an external origin, which is §13 #7. Building it would answer that decision by accident.

  • not measured — anything at all on macOS.

  • measured — every instrument runs from one command now (tools/verify.mjs), which writes a

dated receipt carrying the commit, the host's capabilities and every count, and refuses to say "all held" when any stage was skipped. Its own first version proved why: it probed for tools with --version, which tauri-driver does not answer, and skipped every stage that mattered while reporting all stages held · 5 skipped. A capability probe that errs toward SKIP is the worst kind — the run goes green having tested nothing.

  • measured — the rules compose across an app boundary: handoff-battery, 21 held · 0

failed. Two packages, routing by declaration, an unroutable kind refused by name, acceptance as the only transfer, eviction as the mechanism rather than an optimisation, a terminal package refused when it tries to hand work on, each app's state surviving its own eviction, and one live pane at every observation.

  • corrected — N > 1 is not needed for a second app. The budget limits simultaneous live

panes; two apps, routing, eviction, state and sequential promotion are all provable under N = 1, and §5's zero-pane claim is stronger still. Only simultaneous residency needs §13 #6.

  • found — a grant derived from a package's declaration (produces → offer) makes

authority a consequence of what an app said it was, not a role the shell hands out. Its refusal is defended at three layers and the sabotage that falsifies it must dismantle all three.

  • corrected — receipts are build artifacts, not repository content. One committed

alongside the revision it describes was written before that revision existed and permanently recorded working tree dirty; a receipt now names the tested revision and says loudly when the tree was not clean.

  • stated as a limit — macOS is an explicitly unverified target and its runtime check is a

release gate, not a development blocker. CI compiles and unit-tests on macos-14 and prints, on every run, that it has validated no geometry, no containment and no input — a green tick that reads as "macOS works" would be worse than no job.

  • measured 2026-09-12 — two fixed presentation lanes retain N=1. The integrated

Super battery holds 30 checks, accepted handoff 24. The destination sign agrees with its read frame; the standalone native fullscreen rectangle has zero offset at 1920×1080 / 1×. These runs used an isolated Mutter/XWayland display and software rendering because the locked physical desktop stopped animation frames. No hardware frame-rate, Super runtime-lane routing or macOS claim follows.
